summary.value: This work proposes a simple method which identifies a ``correctness'' vector as the difference between the average representations of incorrect and correct answers, projecting new problems' representations onto the computed vector to extract the LLMs learned evaluation of its own answer's correctness on the problem.

strengths.value:
1. The paper includes sufficient detail to understand the complete experimental and methodological design
2. The text is in general clearly written.

weaknesses.value:
1. Experimental setting: datasets used are mostly synthetic and private. Weak justification was provided for the exclusion of the typically included datasets.
2. Lack of clarity in the description of experiments and results. Figures 3 and 4, in particular, are lacking. Figure 3 is difficult to interpret without an idea of how the baselines perform. Figure 4 is difficult to understand given the hazy decision rule. Table 3 also has some strange values which go unaddressed. Table 3 would benefit greatly from a baseline LLM performance on the immediate task (or a numerically equivalent methodological baseline which naively predicts ``Correct'' at all times). 
3. Lack of explicit motivation or downstream design: the text does not go far to motivate the work. In the same vein, the experimental design is such that the method's downstream utility is hard to gauge: a decision rule, or a process for finding a decision rule, is not described. Instead, results are aggregated for all possible thresholding rules. Correctness prediction is a 2nd-degree task, in that it is a prediction on a prediction. However, its utility in improving its 1st-degree task (Question answering) is not discussed.

questions.value:
1. Figure 4 demonstrates the distributions of your three classes on their correctness scores. We see that, particularly in the 7B case, "Wrong" is entirely overlapped by the other two classes. This means that, given this observation, for any correctness score, one of the other classes will have a higher probability. This means that the optimal maximum likelihood estimation-based prediction would never predict "wrong". In practice, I understand that you are in fact picking a naive score threshold (I suppose two thresholds since you've defined a third ``IDK'' class), and are measuring AUROC over all thresholds. This makes Figure 4 seem strange, however, since score overlap across classes should not be possible with a thresholding decision. Can you comment on the class-distribution interpretation of Figure 4, and clarify how the data in this Figure was compiled?
2. Some of the datasets you use have very high direct task accuracy on modern LLMs. GSM8K, for example, is typically considered too easy a dataset at this point. I would also expect Cities' accuracy to be extremely high on the immediate task, assuming you only used major cities to construct questions. For these datasets, always predicting ``True'' would appear as having very high accuracy. In fact, such a prediction scheme would allow us to always match downstream performance in the correctness classification task. How do your own reported statistics compare with the direct tasks'? For GSM8K, the only public dataset you use, it seems likely to be much weaker. In your main table, you should indicate vanilla-prompted direct-task performance (or the naive classifier performance we get by always predicting ``True'').  
3. In truth, semantically, all single-concept free-form generation problems are effectively multiple choice. This is because in practice, when temperature-sampled (i.e. self-consistency), the LLM will only generate a handful of potential answers. Most of the time, with the exception of very hard datasets, one of the LLMs potential answers will be the correct one. This commonly observed behavior makes your dataset-selection justification hard to buy. In addition, even if there were strong random-selection bias, such a bias would be present in each method's observed performance and so the comparison would remain fair. In fact, this would probably be a good test for training robustness. If 5% of the collected ``True'' datapoints were lucky guesses, would this really impact training substantially? Besides, you can always take public datasets and convert them from multiple-choice to free-form generation by simply not providing the multiple choices in your prompt. Can you either provide experimental results on a few new datasets or provide stronger justification of your experimental design?
4. You present in Figure 3 your method's performance when trained on datasets other than TriviaQA. How does this compare to the assessor?
5. You have a massive volume of training data, which is all high-dimensional. Why not use a standard MLP classifier as an assessor instead of logistic regression? This seems the perfect setting for a softmaxxed MLP. 
6. While the work is not expressly motivated in the text, motivation for such a correctness prediction seems clear: we can estimate answer-verification a priori in order to develop schemes to improve post-training performance. While I understand that this verification scheme is not in scope, it would be trivial to test your method's downstream utility on a binary task such as True-or-False questions, where if the classification is categorized by your method as incorrect then the true answer must be the single alternative class. Effectively, you could procedurally generate the ``True'' class for each question and test whether this answer is correct, making your method immediately applicable to the task. I'd like to see this on something like FOLIO, which is True/Unknown/False (you can use your "IDK" for maybe, or just cut out all the "Unknown"-labelled problems from the dataset). 
7. In Table 3, you often report sub-random performances (less than 0.5). What is happening in the models to produce such class inversions? 
8. I don't understand why you don't commit to a single decision boundary. In training, the identification of an optimal boundary should be simple to find. In truth, this method is unusable without committing to a boundary, and your experimental results are all weakened and made less interpretable by requiring an AUROC measurement.

We thank the reviewer for their attention to detail. Below we respond to each *comment/weakness*, and hope that you can reconsider your score in light of our discussion.

*Experimental setting: datasets used are mostly synthetic and private. Weak justification was provided for the exclusion of the typically included datasets.* 

All datasets we use are either public benchmarks (TriviaQA, GSM8K) or are generated from public, CC-licensed tables (Cities, Notable People, Medals, Math Operations; Table 1 and Sec. 4.1.1). We would like to clarify that none of them are private, and they were chosen them because they (i) allow open-ended answers with fully automatic grading, (ii) give mid-range accuracy for our models (Table 5), so both correct and incorrect classes are reasonably well populated, and (iii) attempt to reduce exact benchmark memorisation by using our own templates over public sources. 

*Lack of clarity in the description of experiments and results. Figures 3 and 4, in particular, are lacking. Figure 3 is difficult to interpret without an idea of how the baselines perform. Figure 4 is difficult to understand given the hazy decision rule. Table 3 also has some strange values which go unaddressed. Table 3 would benefit greatly from a baseline LLM performance on the immediate task (or a numerically equivalent methodological baseline which naively predicts ``Correct'' at all times).*

We warmly thank the reviewer for the suggestions and agree that some figures can be made clearer. To clarify: Figure 3 reports only the performance of our correctness direction, and the corresponding assessor baselines (trained on TriviaQA) are already in Table 3, with extended results in Appendix B.3. We will make the Figure 3 caption more self-contained and explicitly cross-reference these tables. We also plan to add an assessor heatmap (assessors trained per dataset, mirroring Fig. 3) in the appendix, which will take some time. Figure 4 is purely descriptive: it shows the histogram of scalar scores (projections on the correctness direction) for three types of answers (“right”, “wrong”, “IDK”), not the outputs of a three-class classifier. Overlap between these histograms is therefore expected and compatible with a single-threshold decision rule. We will clarify this in the caption, emphasising that the point of the plot is to show that “IDK” answers concentrate at the lowest scores, supporting the “confidence” interpretation. For Table 3, we will (i) add a short explanation about entries that are close to random performance (around 0.5), (ii) bring up direct task accuracies from Table 5 in the main text near Table 3, and (iii) include, in the appendix, a simple “always correct” baseline and a fixed-threshold version of our method for ease of comparison.

*Lack of explicit motivation or downstream design: the text does not go far to motivate the work. In the same vein, the experimental design is such that the method's downstream utility is hard to gauge: a decision rule, or a process for finding a decision rule, is not described. Instead, results are aggregated for all possible thresholding rules. Correctness prediction is a 2nd-degree task, in that it is a prediction on a prediction. However, its utility in improving its 1st-degree task (Question answering) is not discussed.*

We thank this reviewer's comment on the framing and theory of change of our paper. In its current form, our primary goal is scientific: we want to test whether a linearly accessible, pre-generation correctness signal exists in LLM internals, how strong it is, and how it generalises across models and datasets. This is somewhat different from proposing a complete deployment pipeline, as we expect any practical system to combine multiple signals (e.g., internal probes, sampling-based methods, verbalised confidence) rather than rely on a single probe. Rather, we see it more as sketching out the contours, limitations, and mechanisms for a possible step to include in such a pipeline, which may have utility in improving the 1st-degree task.

AUROC is standard in classicfication and probing work and directly answers our core question about separability without committing to any particular application-specific operating point. Finding a decision rule is a simple matter of choosing the threshold that maximises accuracy on a dataset. We will state this more explicitly in the introduction and conclusion, and we have also included accuracy results for a fixed decision rule in Table 7. 

[Cont. below]

We apologise for the confusion. Figure 4 does not depict the output of a three-class classifier. For each model and dataset, we (i) train a binary direction on “correct” vs “not correct”, treating “I don’t know” as incorrect, and then (ii) plot the scalar scores for those examples, grouped by their actual answer types (“right”, “wrong”, “IDK”). The overlap across the three histograms simply reflects that the binary score is not perfectly discriminative, which is consistent with the non-perfect AUROCs we report. The figure is intended to show that “IDK” answers cluster at the low-score tail, which supports the view of this direction as a confidence axis, not to define a 3-way decision rule. We will clarify this in the caption and main text.

*Some of the datasets you use have very high direct task accuracy on modern LLMs. [...]*

For the open models we use, accuracies are far from saturated. As shown in Table 5, GSM8K accuracy ranges from 10.7% to 44.3%, and Cities from 45.8% to 80.3%, depending on the model, so there is substantial room for both correct and incorrect examples in all datasets. We will move key numbers from Table 5 into the main text near Table 3 to make this clearer. A naive “always correct” classifier has AUROC = 0.5 by definition, and our correctness directions exceed this on all factual datasets (TriviaQA, Notable People, Cities, Math Operations, Medals) across all models (Table 3). 

In the appendix, we provide a new Table 7 (in App. B.3), which reports the accuracy of a thresholded classifier based on the correctness direction, both with a TriviaQA-trained threshold and with dataset-specific thresholds. This makes the comparison more concrete: on TriviaQA, for example, our classifier attains accuracies around 0.67–0.75, while an “always correct” baseline would match the underlying QA accuracy but still have AUROC 0.5. We therefore see AUROC as the right primary metric for our scientific question but that reasonable decision rules are available when one wants to trade off errors in practice!

We believe that an MLP assessor would further increase capacity but not significantly change the interpretability question, so we chose to keep the baseline set simple and focused. We hope this clears up the motivation, and frames our contribution within the hopes of many other mechanistic interpretability works which aim to approach this high-dimensional data as a space containing high-level concepts which can be represented linearly as directions (LRH).

*While the work is not expressly motivated in the text, motivation for such a correctness prediction seems clear: we can estimate answer-verification a priori in order to develop schemes to improve post-training performance. While I understand that this verification scheme is not in scope, it would be trivial to test your method's downstream utility on a binary task such as True-or-False questions, where if the classification is categorized by your method as incorrect then the true answer must be the single alternative class. Effectively, you could procedurally generate the ``True'' class for each question and test whether this answer is correct, making your method immediately applicable to the task. I'd like to see this on something like FOLIO, which is True/Unknown/False (you can use your "IDK" for maybe, or just cut out all the "Unknown"-labelled problems from the dataset).*

We agree that applying the probe in a true/false setting such as FOLIO is an interesting direction. Doing so, however, requires extra design choices (how to construct the alternative class, how to integrate with the dataset, how to choose thresholds) and additional compute. In this paper we focus on characterising the internal correctness signal itself (where it appears in the network, how strong it is, and how it generalises, and so on) rather than optimising a full verification pipeline. We will expand the discussion section to emphasise that we expect practical systems to combine our probe with other signals rather than rely on it alone!

*In Table 3, you often report sub-random performances (less than 0.5). What is happening in the models to produce such class inversions?*

In Table 3, the few AUROC values below 0.5 are all close to random (typically 0.45–0.50) and arise in settings where the signal is weak (notably some assessor scores on Math Operations and GSM8K, and one GSM8K value for our direction on Llama 3.3 70B). For our direction, AUROC < 0.5 simply means that, for that model–dataset pair, the learned scalar score is mildly anti-correlated with correctness. We suspect this can happen because (i) the underlying signal is very weak (so the noise from finite samples), and/or (ii) the direction, which is only defined up to sign, ends up slightly “flipped” relative to how we would orient it if we optimised sign per dataset. We very carefully do not post-hoc flip the sign per dataset, to avoid any cherry-picking and to keep the analysis comparable across settings. We will add a short explanation of this behaviour to the text.

*I don't understand why you don't commit to a single decision boundary. In training, the identification of an optimal boundary should be simple to find. In truth, this method is unusable without committing to a boundary, and your experimental results are all weakened and made less interpretable by requiring an AUROC measurement.*

We use AUROC because it is threshold-free, widely used in probing work, and directly measures how linearly separable the two classes are, which is our main scientific question. In any deployment, a practitioner would choose a decision boundary using a small validation set, tuned to some preferred trade-off between false positives and false negatives. To address the reviewer’s concern, we have added an appendix table (new Table 7, in Appendix B.3) that commits to concrete thresholds, where for each model and training dataset, we (i) choose a single scalar threshold that maximises accuracy on that training dataset, and (ii) report the resulting classifier accuracy across all test datasets. The “TriviaQA” columns show the case where the threshold and direction are both trained on TriviaQA and then transferred to other datasets, while the “Itself” columns show the case where both the direction and the threshold are trained on the target dataset.

What happens when you do this? In-distribution, a simple threshold on the correctness direction yields pretty sensible accuracies (e.g., around 0.67–0.75 on TriviaQA, and up to around 0.83–0.96 on the synthetic factual datasets), which is around the AUROCs you see in Table 3. Then OOD, when we transfer the TriviaQA-trained threshold to other datasets, accuracies fall in line with the cross-dataset AUROCs: they remain above random for other factual datasets, but stay around chance on GSM8K (~0.50), which reinforces our conclusion that the question-only correctness signal does not transfer well to multi-step reasoning. We hope this gives confidence that (i) it is straightforward to instantiate our probe as a thresholded classifier with a single decision boundary, and (ii) AUROC is still the more informative metric for our purposes, because it describes the underlying correctness signal independent of class imbalance and threshold calibration.

This gives some evidence that models store a relatively accessible “knowledge correctness” signal before generation, while the success of multi-step mathematical reasoning depends on computations that are not yet encoded at question-only time, or are not linearly separable. We will clarify this framing in the Introduction and Discussion so that readers do not interpret the limited GSM8K performance as a failure of the method, but rather as a boundary of the phenomenon we are studying.

*Inconsistent Signal Across Layers: The appendix (e.g., Figure 9) shows that the signal peak for different task types appears in different model layers. This suggests the model may lack a unified "self-awareness" center, making the practical deployment of a single, simple probe unstable.*

We did not intend to claim that there is a single “self-awareness center” layer. In fact, many interpretability works (such as the ones we cite in our related works) find that useful high-level features emerge gradually and are strongest in middle to late layers rather than being localised to a single layer. Our results show a fairly consistent pattern across models: early layers perform poorly, the correctness signal rises around the middle, and a range of nearby layers achieve similar AUROC (Figure 9). In the main text we explicitly select the best layer on TriviaQA, **but importantly in Appendix B.7 we also report the “first good enough” layer that reaches 90% of the best TriviaQA performance, and this lies in a fairly broad band.** This suggests that the signal is distributed across several adjacent layers.

Moreover, the fact that the peak performance for some of the ""specific"" datasets (e.g., Math Operations) appears in different layer from the peak for TriviaQA is likely due to the linear probe for the specific dataset learning dataset-specific features that are connected to performance on that dataset but may not transfer to other datasets, which makes them poorly generalisable (as can be seen in Figure 6).

For practical use, one could aggregate projections from a small window of layers or simply choose the first “good enough” layer instead of the exact optimum. 

*Oversimplified Definition of Correctness: The study treats correctness as a binary label and operates in a deterministic (zero-temperature) setting. This ignores the stochasticity of answers and the ambiguity of correctness in real-world scenarios.*

This is right! We agree that the fully-fledge construct of correctness can be stochastic and graded in realistic deployments, and we do not claim that our binary, temperature-0 setup fully captures this complexity. We intentionally chose a highly controlled setting in order to isolate the existence and structure of a latent correctness signal, so as to avoid conflating epistemic uncertainty with some more unwieldy artifacts such as sampling noise or ambiguous labels. Zero temperature and binary labels remove aleatoric randomness from the target, which lets us ask (what we feel is) a fairly clean research question: “Given this deterministic policy, are activations before generation linearly predictive of whether the model’s chosen answer will match the gold label?” We see this as a necessary first step before tackling more complex regimes that involve multiple samples per question, soft correctness scores, or non-binary grading, which some works may have jumped to already, and discuss this as a limitation in Section 6. *Why does it fail on reasoning? This is the most critical question. Is it because the correctness signal for reasoning only emerges during the generation process, or is this type of signal inherently non-linear? This points to an important direction for future research.*

We fully agree that understanding the GSM8K failure is central and we thank the reviewer for articulating the key hypotheses. At the moment, our current experiments cannot definitively distinguish between “signal only emerges during generation” and “signal is present but non-linear,” so we are careful not to over-interpret the result. Our findings suggest two plausible explanations:

**Temporal explanation.** For multi-step reasoning, whether the model will succeed depends on the internal chain of computations that unfolds during generation. At question-only time, the representation may encode problem type and surface difficulty, but not the detailed trajectory of reasoning, so a correctness signal may only become linearly separable later in the chain-of-thought.

**Geometric / non-linear explanation.** It is also possible that for reasoning tasks the relevant correctness features exist at question-only time but are not well approximated by a single linear direction. This is consistent with our sample-size study (Figure 5), where increasing training data for GSM8K does not close the performance gap, suggesting that limited data is not the main issue.

A natural extension here is to repeat our analysis along the full generation trajectory, or to compare linear probes with higher-capacity non-linear probes on reasoning tasks. We see our GSM8K result as pointing directly to this future work, and add this to our limitations section as future work.

*Practical value of "white-box" access? This method requires access to internal model activations and necessitates training a probe for a specific model and layer. In practical deployment, what are its main advantages in terms of computational overhead and maintenance costs compared to post-generation detection methods? Furthermore, since the main experiment only proves its generalization is significantly better than the baseline, but poorer performance on the corresponding datasets, does this also imply the method might just be a mediocre choice rather than the optimal solution?*

Our primary goal in this paper is to gain scientific insight into what current LLMs encode internally, rather than to propose a single best practical detector. That said, white-box probes of the kind we study do have concrete advantages in settings where internals are available, such as open models or on-prem deployments. Once activations are cached, our probe reduces to a single linear projection per example. Training the probe means learning one d-dimensional vector on cached activations, which takes minutes on CPU, and inference is much cheaper than any sampling-based or post-generation method that requires multiple answers. This makes it a natural choice for a pre-generation or early-warning filter under tight token budgets, which can be followed by more expensive post-generation checks on questions flagged as uncertain.

We have some new results which provide some evidence for this, actually! In Table 7 (Appendix B.3), we report accuracies for a thresholded classifier based on the correctness direction, with a single scalar threshold chosen on the training dataset and then transferred to other datasets. This shows that the probe can be used as a simple, concrete decision mechanism, and that it retains the robustness patterns suggested by AUROC. While some black-box assessors achieve slightly higher in-distribution AUROC on TriviaQA, our results show that they overfit and degrade substantially under domain shift, whereas the correctness direction generalises much better to new factual datasets. For deployments where safety or distribution shift is a significant concern, this can matter more or less than marginal in-distribution gains, and our probe may not be the optimal practical solution in isolation. Rather, we see it as a complementary white-box tool that reveals a correctness signal in model internals and can form one component of a broader ensemble that combines white-box and black-box uncertainty estimators.

We agree that verbalised confidence alone is not a strong baseline! This is precisely why we also include assessor baselines (logistic regression and XGBoost) trained on model-independent question embeddings (Sec. 4.1.3, App. B.3), which are stronger and widely used in the predictability literature (e.g., Hernández-Orallo et al., 2022; Pacchiardi et al., 2024; 2025). Furthermore, our goal is not to claim a new state-of-the-art calibration method, but to ask whether a one-dimensional direction in the residual stream can meaningfully predict correctness compared to standard external baselines. 

*In terms of factual data, where the answers are short, the question-only setting does not seem to have considerable efficiency advantage, compared to the one with answer generation.*

We see the question-only setting primarily as a scientific probe rather than as a deployment scheme (which would likely employ some mixture of white- and black- box methods). As we state in the introduction, our main aim is to test whether residual stream activations immediately after reading the question contain a latent correctness signal, not to minimise inference cost. That said, once activations are available (e.g., because the model is already being called for another purpose), our probe is extremely cheap: learning the d-dimensional direction is a one-shot computation on cached activations (<3 minutes on CPU for 10k samples), and applying it is a single linear projection per question (Sec. 4.1). By contrast, several existing uncertainty methods require multiple generations or additional prompts.

*The paper completely misses critically-related work. There are other papers considering the same kind of probing: [1-5]. Those papers show some very similar results.*

We thank the reviewer for pointing out [1–5]; these works are indeed closely related and have integrated them into Further Related Work and Appendix A. Taken together with our results, we think they support a consistent picture and show that internal states at question time already contain information about future factuality or hallucination risk. Our contribution in this cluster of works is to show that this signal can be captured in a particularly constrained and interpretable form, and to characterise where it generalises and where it fails.

Concretely, our work differs from [1–5] in three main ways which we believe are important:

**Stricter and simpler probe.** Several of [1–5] use richer features of the generation process (e.g. early generated tokens, multi-step trajectories, or question+context encodings) and more expressive classifiers. We deliberately work in a stricter setting: a single one-dimensional difference-of-means direction in the residual stream of one layer, computed from question-only activations before any token is generated. Showing that this minimal probe already predicts correctness across datasets and models strengthens the case that correctness/confidence is a linearly accessible internal quantity, not just something recoverable with complex readouts. We build this case showing that it even has advantages against more advanced classifier baselines, which we hope makes clear that our choice of a minimal setting was deliberately considered.

**Systematic cross-dataset and cross-model analysis of self-correctness.** Several cited works target hallucination or answerability in reading comprehension with context passages, or knowledge at the entity level (e.g. “all questions about Napoleon”). We instead study per-question self-correctness for free-form factual QA across six open-source models from three families (7B–70B), and we do so with a fixed layer per model chosen on TriviaQA. We then systematically map how a single TriviaQA-trained direction transfers to various factual domains (Table 3, Fig. 3, App. B.5–B.6), including failures on GSM8K. We think this experimental design gives a clearer picture of how broad the internal correctness signal is and when it breaks, which is our focus in this work.
